description.p: Machines manages the QEMU/KVM virtual machines of a libvirt connection, the system one or your user session, built with GTK 4 and libadwaita.

ul.li: Start, shut down, pause, save to disk, reboot and force off machines, and follow their state as it changes

A built-in VNC and SPICE console that scales the guest's display to the window and passes the keyboard and pointer through, with sound, clipboard sharing, USB redirection and 3D acceleration over SPICE
A serial console shown as text
New machines from an installation ISO or an existing disk image, with a disk in libvirt's default storage pool, set up for the system on the ISO
Processors, memory, autostart, boot order and the CD-ROM drive changed from the details page
Graphs of what a running machine uses of the host's processors, memory, disks and network
Processor model, topology and pinning, huge pages, and BIOS or UEFI firmware with Secure Boot
Machines renamed, and cloned with copies of their disks
Snapshots of a machine's disks, and of its memory while it runs, to revert to
Disks, CD/DVD drives, network interfaces, display and video card, and USB and PCI devices of the host added and changed from the details page
Storage pools, disks of the host and virtual networks
A machine's XML definition, edited by hand

description.p: The details have a Passthrough group for Looking Glass, the memory balloon, hiding the hypervisor from the guest, and the host's keyboard and mouse. Looking Glass gets the SPICE listener and screen it needs, and is turned on only where its client is installed. Advanced settings reach from the machine type and power actions to disk and network card tuning, and the scripts libvirt runs as a machine starts and stops can be edited, saved through an administrator's password. The definition opens in a resizable editor with XML highlighting, line numbers, and find and replace. A stopped machine opens on its details and shows its screen once it starts, and a machine that cannot start for want of huge pages says how many are missing.

A disk or network card whose settings change at the next start is marked as such, and a setting libvirt refuses shows as it was. Settings QEMU cannot have, such as the host's system information on the user's own connection, are no longer offered.

The window no longer waits on libvirt as a connection or serial console closes, as a screenshot is saved, or as the details look at the host's devices and scripts. Usage graphs no longer take a sample from the machine shown before, and the New Virtual Machine and Add Storage dialogs free their memory once closed.

A click in the console gives the virtual machine the shortcuts the desktop would otherwise take, such as Super and Alt+Tab, until Ctrl+Alt releases the keyboard, which the console says as it takes them. Fullscreen has a button in the main window too, and in fullscreen the machine's controls, with the keys to send, come down from the top edge of the screen: for a moment as fullscreen starts, while the pointer is at the edge, and at a tap there on a touch screen. The serial console says so while nothing has arrived from the guest.

A libvirt daemon that stops answering now shows as a lost connection instead of leaving the window waiting. SPICE is offered only where QEMU has its SPICE modules, and a machine that cannot start without them says what to install. The console redraws only what changed of the guest's screen, and screen readers know it by the machine's name.

New virtual machines boot with the firmware chosen for them: BIOS, UEFI, or UEFI with Secure Boot, which is the default where the host's firmware has it, as Windows 11 requires. Their disk goes in the storage pool chosen for it, which shows its free space, and their processors are cores of one socket, so that Windows uses all of them.

The serial console is offered only to machines with a serial port, which is added and removed with the other devices. The sidebar selects a machine on a click, no longer as the pointer passes over it. Fullscreen works from any page, with F11 too, and going back to the list leaves it. The user session explains why it has no virtual networks instead of failing to make one, and a keyboard shortcuts dialog lists what the keyboard does.
